title_topic: Frailty and the older surgical patient
summary: A consultant-level look at frailty in older surgical patients for anaesthetists and intensivists. SNAP-3 (BJA 2025; 7,129 UK patients aged 60 and over, 214 hospitals) found that about one in five were frail, and outcomes worsened from a Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score of 4 upwards. Frailty, more than multimorbidity, drove length of stay, delirium and mortality. The CFS is quick and about as accurate as a modified Fried index (adjusted odds ratio 2.51 for death or new disability at 90 days in a 702-patient Canadian cohort), but it is a baseline population risk marker, poorly validated in younger people or those with stable single-system disability, and it says nothing about the operation. Prehabilitation trials in frail patients (Carli, JAMA Surg 2020; McIsaac's PREHAB, BJA 2022) were neutral. A supervised in-hospital programme in a non-frail colorectal cohort (PREHAB, JAMA Surg 2023) reduced severe complications (17.1 versus 29.7 percent). A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 186 trials favoured exercise, but with very low certainty. Comprehensive geriatric assessment reduces discharge to a higher level of care (Cochrane 2018, mostly hip fracture). The CPOC/BGS 2021 guideline, still current, sets the UK standard: CFS for everyone over 65, CGA and cognitive assessment at CFS 5 or more, and daily 4AT screening. For delirium, regional versus general anaesthesia made no difference (REGAIN, RAGA). EEG guidance was neutral in ENGAGES, and Balanced found no mortality difference between BIS 50 and 35, yet ESAIC 2024 still weakly suggests EEG monitoring. B-Free (benzodiazepine restriction in cardiac surgery) was neutral. Shared decision-making should follow Montgomery and centre on function and going home. ANZICS registry data (BJA 2025) link frailty to shorter long-term survival after postoperative ICU admission (adjusted hazard ratio 2.33).
takeaways: Document a CFS, but read it as a population risk marker: risk climbs from CFS 4, and the score says nothing about the operation.
Prehabilitation is reasonable, but the trials in frail patients are neutral; supervised programmes with good adherence look best.
Regional versus general anaesthesia doesn't change delirium. Avoid delirium-provoking drugs and excessive depth, and use multicomponent prevention.
Get a geriatrician involved early; the best evidence for comprehensive geriatric assessment is in hip fracture.
Before surgery, talk about function and going home, and agree the ceiling of treatment, including ICU.
